query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The maintenance of structural and chemical stability in equiatomic, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is governed by kinetic barriers to atomic diffusion that counteract the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation. In other words, if the lattice distortion and configurational complexity impose sufficiently high kinetic barriers, then even at temperatures up to 1923 K the solid solution remains intact.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles comprised of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, initially crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Expose the nanoparticles to controlled catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions while incrementally increasing the temperature from 473 K up to 1923 K.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert or well‐controlled reactive atmospheres with constant pressure, replicating actual catalytic and thermoelectric environments in the 473–1923 K range.
generation.structural_mediator: High lattice distortion and low atomic diffusivity arising from severe configurational disorder.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the high configurational entropy and lattice distortion impose kinetic barriers that limit atomic motion, thus preventing phase separation. Even as thermal energy increases, these kinetic limitations dominate until a critical threshold is reached, beyond which diffusion may overcome the barriers and lead to elemental segregation. The balance between entropic stabilization and diffusion-mediated segregation determines phase stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with sufficiently high kinetic barriers should retain a single-phase structure with minimal chemical redistribution up to a critical temperature within the 473–1923 K range, with observable signs of segregation only when thermal energy overcomes these barriers.
generation.baseline: The initial, well-mixed, single-phase high-entropy alloy state at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions where environmental factors do not excessively lower the diffusion barriers; a breakdown is expected if the temperature exceeds the critical threshold or if reactive conditions promote diffusion, leading to detectable phase segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperature and the quantitative influence of the catalytic environment on the kinetic barriers remain uncertain and require further determination through combined experimental and simulation studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ studies by progressively heating high-entropy alloy nanoparticles under both catalytic and thermoelectric test conditions. Monitor the evolution of their phase composition and elemental distribution using real-time X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM), while simultaneously running atomistic simulations to estimate diffusion kinetics and segregation energies.
measurements: XRD peak analysis to detect the emergence of multiple phases
In situ TEM imaging to observe any elemental redistribution or phase segregation
Calculation of diffusion coefficients and simulated kinetic barriers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If experimental measurements show significant phase segregation or detectable chemical inhomogeneity at temperatures where the hypothesis predicts high kinetic barriers (i.e. before the expected critical temperature is reached), then the hypothesis—that kinetic limitations alone govern stability—would be falsified.

The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In this study, we present in situ atomic-scale evidence that a random solid solution (RSS) structure enables AuCu NWs to exhibit superplasticity with ~260% uniform elongation and ultrahigh strength of ~6 GPa. We discovered that the excellent properties originate from the chemical inhomogeneity (similar to that of high-entropy alloys), which leads to widely distributed and overlapping energy barriers for multiple plasticity mechanisms and enables the AuCu alloy NWs to exhibit several unconventional plastic deformation modes, such as an ultrahigh density of deformation-induced HCP lamellae (including 2H and 4H phases), zigzag-like nanotwins, and reversible FCC–HCP phase transition. Polymorphism, which refers to the ability of a solid material to exist in more than one crystal structure, is widely observed in many materials including polymers, minerals and metals. The polymorphic transition is a well-known yet critical phenomenon in nature and surprisingly, polymorphs with identical compositions can have different physical, chemical and mechanical properties due to different structural characteristics, which have attracted considerable attention over the last few decades. Pressure and temperature are usually controlling parameters for inducing these transitions by altering the atomic and/or electronic structures and creating novel materials. For example, carbon can take on graphite and diamond under different pressures and temperatures.

New high throughput experiments are needed, especially for structural materials. And new strategies are needed to quickly navigate the winding, narrow path between properties that depend on composition, and those that depend sensitively on both composition and exquisitely designed microstructures. Acquiring new fundamental data is also essential. Current scientific efforts are built on data and knowledge collected more than 50 years ago. AbstractThe high-entropy transition metal borides containing a random distribution of five or more constituent metallic elements offer novel opportunities in designing materials that show crystalline phase stability, high strength, and thermal oxidation resistance under extreme conditions. We present a comprehensive theoretical and experimental investigation of prototypical high-entropy boride (HEB) materials such as (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti)B2 and (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Zr)B2 under extreme environments of pressures and temperatures. The theoretical tools include modeling elastic properties by special quasi-random structures that predict a bulk modulus of 288 GPa and a shear modulus of 215 GPa at ambient conditions. HEB samples were synthesized under high pressures and high temperatures and studied to 9.5 GPa and 2273 K in a large-volume pressure cell. The thermal equation of state measurement yielded a bulk modulus of 276 GPa, in excellent agreement with theory. The measured compressive yield strength by radial X-ray diffraction technique in a diamond anvil cell was 28 GPa at a pressure of 65 GPa, which is a significant fraction of the shear modulus at high pressures. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple elements in near-equiatomic proportions hold great promise in heterogeneous catalysis because of their exceptional physicochemical properties governed by synergy. Herein, we prepared PtPdCoCuNi HEA nanoparticles via a one-step colloid-based route and tested their catalytic performance for nitrobenzene hydrogenation to aniline. The SiO2 supported PtPdCoCuNi displays 93.9% yield of aniline at 80 °C, which is 2.11 times that of PtPd/SiO2. Even at room temperature, a 47.4% yield of aniline is attained with the PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst. DRIFTS experiments indicate formation of isolated Pt and Pd sites after alloying the transition metals and evidence a stronger interaction between the HEA catalyst and nitrobenzene. Both XPS data and DFT calculations disclose charge transfer to Pt and Pd species, which eventually enhance the interaction between nitrobenzene and the isolated metal sites and the hydrogenation activity as well.
